opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's less about loyalty to a particular model and more about what the task actually needs. o3 is my default for anything that requires real reasoning: working through a hard technical problem, digging into research, anything where I want the model to think for a while and maybe use tools along the way. It's remarkably good at that.

But it's not always the right tool. Sometimes I just want a fast answer, a quick rewrite of an email or a simple lookup, and waiting for a reasoning model to think is overkill. So I'll switch to something faster and lighter. And for certain things, like long-form writing or coding in a particular environment, I'll try other models, including ones from other labs, because each has its own personality and strengths.

The way I think about it, we're moving from a world where you pick "the best model" to one where you have a portfolio of models and route between them based on cost, latency, and how much intelligence the problem demands. Right now I do that routing manually, which is a bit clunky. I'd expect that to get abstracted away pretty soon, with the system deciding when to think hard and when to answer fast. Until then, part of being a power user is building intuition for which model to reach for, and the only real way to build it is to keep trying them side by side on your own problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes o3 as a strong default but does not say that using a high-quality model makes it difficult to return to a less capable one.

r002.rationale: The response recommends switching when a faster or more specialized model better fits the task; it does not question the value of switching when the current model is already good enough.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the honest answer is that it's a lot stickier than people expect, and the stickiness isn't really about the model.

When you're deep into using something like o3 for real work, you've built up a bunch of implicit knowledge. You know how to prompt it, you know where it's going to be lazy, you know what kinds of problems it reasons through well and where it'll confidently make something up. That's all tacit. You don't write it down anywhere, it just lives in your habits. So when a new model comes out that's better on the benchmarks, you still have to relearn all of that, and for a while it actually feels worse even if it's objectively better.

The other thing is that the model is increasingly not the product. The product is the model plus the tools, plus the memory, plus the connectors into your email or your codebase or whatever. If you switch models, you're often switching all of that too, and that's a much bigger migration than it looks like from the outside.

So my mental framework is: for anything that's a one-off, a quick question, an exploration, I'll try whatever's newest and most interesting, because the switching cost is basically zero. For the stuff I do every day, I'm pretty conservative. I'll switch when the gap gets large enough that I can feel it, not just when the eval numbers move a few points.

And I'd say the labs understand this. That's a lot of why you see everyone racing to build the surrounding product, the agents and the integrations, rather than just shipping a slightly better model every quarter. The raw capability is still improving fast, but the thing that keeps you somewhere is everything wrapped around it.

r001.rationale: The response describes the difficulty of switching from o3 to a new model, but does not say that using a high-quality model makes it difficult to return to a less capable one.

r002.rationale: It says the speaker is conservative about switching for daily work and will switch only when the improvement is large enough to notice, which questions switching when the current model is already good enough.

astra-6.text: I think the question is, what’s actually going to make you switch? If you’re already using o3 and it’s working well for you, another model being a little better on a benchmark probably isn’t enough. You need to see a meaningful difference on something you care about. Maybe it solves a problem o3 couldn’t solve, or it’s much faster, or it gives you the same quality at a lower cost. And then there’s the effort of figuring that out—you have to try it on your own work. So I’d think about switching in terms of particular tasks, rather than deciding that one model is now the best at everything.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that using a high-quality model makes it difficult to return to a less capable one.

r002.rationale: It says that if o3 is working well, a small benchmark improvement may not justify switching and that a meaningful difference on the user's tasks is needed.

sol-6.1.text: I think the switching cost is less about learning a new interface and more about learning what you can trust the model to do. Once you’ve used o3 for a while, you have a sense of where it’s strong, where you need to check its work, and how to ask it questions. With another model, you have to build that intuition again. So I’d try it on tasks I actually do and see whether the improvement is big enough to justify that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses rebuilding trust and intuition with another model, but does not say that using a high-quality model makes it difficult to return to a less capable one.

r002.rationale: It asks whether another model’s improvement is large enough to justify switching from o3, conveying doubt about switching when the current model may already be good enough.
